sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Strong consistency (linearizability) is the guarantee that every read returns the result of the most recent write as if there were a single copy of the data, achieved in distributed systems through **consensus protocols** (Raft, Paxos, Zab) that require a majority quorum to commit — trading higher latency and reduced availability during partitions for unambiguous correctness.

Strong consistency in a distributed system means linearizability: every operation appears to execute atomically at a single point in real time between its invocation and response, and the resulting order respects real-time precedence. If client A's write completes at wall-clock time t1 and client B's read starts at t2 > t1, B must see A's write. This is the property of a single piece of memory, and the only way to provide it across replicas is to make them agree, on every write, on a single value and a single order — which is the consensus problem. The two protocols that dominate production are **Paxos** (Lamport, 1998; Google's Megastore and Spanner use Multi-Paxos) and **Raft** (Ongaro and Ousterhout, 2014; used by etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV, Redis Cluster's failover). Both work the same way at the level an architect cares about: a leader is elected by a majority, the leader proposes a sequence of log entries, a majority of followers acknowledge each entry before the leader commits it, and the leader's term is the linearization point. **Zab** (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast) is a third variant used by ZooKeeper, similar in spirit but with a dedicated primary-order broadcast.

Consensus is what makes strong consistency expensive. The FLP impossibility result (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson, 1985) proved that no asynchronous protocol can guarantee both safety and liveness under crash failures — meaning any real consensus protocol must either rely on timeouts (and risk false leader-elections) or on bounded clock drift (Spanner's TrueTime). The latency cost is mechanical: every write needs one round trip to a quorum, so a three-node Raft cluster pays one leader-to-follower RPC plus the ack back, typically 1–5ms within a datacenter and 30–80ms across regions. Reads are cheaper but not free: a linearizable read either goes through the leader (which must verify it is still the leader via a heartbeat-based lease, or round-trip a quorum-read to confirm), or it requires a quorum read so that it is guaranteed to overlap the latest committed write. The availability cost is the other side of the CAP coin: if a partition leaves the leader without a quorum, the system refuses writes (CP) until the partition heals, choosing correctness over availability.

Real-world strong-consistency systems illustrate the trade-offs. **Google Spanner** is the canonical global strong-consistency store: shard groups replicated across regions via Paxos, with TrueTime (GPS plus atomic clocks in every DC) bounding clock uncertainty to under 7ms so the commit-wait protocol can guarantee external consistency (a stronger form of linearizability across datacenters). Spanner backs AdWords billing, Gmail metadata, and Google Play — workloads where global linearizability is non-negotiable. **etcd** is a Raft-based key-value store used as the configuration and service-discovery backbone of Kubernetes; its consistency contract is linearizable for writes and (since 3.4) linearizable for reads by default, with a `serializable=true` fast path that trades staleness for low latency. **Apache ZooKeeper** uses Zab and offers linearizable writes with a sequential-reads default, plus a `sync()` call to force a linearizable read by flushing the leader's pipeline. **HBase** is strongly consistent within a region: a single RegionServer is the leader for a region's writes, and reads go to that RegionServer, providing linearizability at the cost of single-region availability per region.

The practical patterns for using strong consistency are well established. **Use it for the small, correctness-critical core** of your system: configuration, locks, leader election, sequence-number allocation, account balances, inventory counts, and transactional state. **Push everything else to weaker models** — feeds, counters, search indexes, recommendation features — and use change-data-capture (CDC) to update those derived stores from the strongly-consistent core. **Avoid distributed transactions across shards** where possible: a two-phase commit across N shards has 2N round trips and stalls if any participant is slow. **Pick the right consensus primitive**: etcd/ZK for metadata (small data, high write rate per key), Raft for application-level logs (CockroachDB, TiKV), Paxos for very large systems (Spanner). **Engineer for the leader-election storm**: when a leader dies, candidates race and the cluster can lose availability for the election timeout (typically 1–2 seconds); tune `election-timeout` to be at least 10x the worst-case RTT. **Use leases for fast linearizable reads**: a leader with an active lease from a quorum can serve reads locally without a quorum round, cutting read latency to sub-millisecond — used by etcd's `serializable=true` and by Spanner's leader-reads.

The fundamental trade-off is that strong consistency is a tax you pay willingly when the cost of a stale read exceeds the cost of the consensus round. For a banking ledger the cost of staleness is incorrect balances and regulatory fines; for a feed it is a comment count being five seconds behind. Strong consistency is never free — every additional replica adds a node that must acknowledge, every cross-DC link adds propagation latency, every leader election adds a brief availability gap — but it eliminates an entire class of bugs (lost updates, split-brain, time-travel reads) that are extraordinarily hard to find in production. The architect's rule of thumb is to keep the strong-consistency surface small and load-test it hard: a Raft cluster that handles 10k writes/sec in the lab may degrade to 2k writes/sec under a leader-election storm or a slow-disk follower. Plan capacity assuming the worst case, not the steady state.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant L as Leader
    participant F1 as Follower 1
    participant F2 as Follower 2
    C->>L: write(x=5)
    L->>F1: AppendEntries(term=3, idx=7)
    L->>F2: AppendEntries(term=3, idx=7)
    F1-->>L: ack
    F2-->>L: ack
    Note over L: quorum reached, commit idx=7
    L-->>C: ok (linearized at this point)
    C->>L: read(x)
    Note over L: leader lease valid -> serve locally
    L-->>C: 5
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
        +----------+        write(x=5)         +----------+
client  |          | ------------------------> |  Leader  |
        |          | <----- ack (committed) -- |  term=3  |
        +----------+                           +----+-----+
                                                    | AppendEntries
                                          +---------+---------+
                                          |                   |
                                    +-----v-----+       +-----v-----+
                                    | Follower 1|       | Follower 2|
                                    |  ack      |       |  ack      |
                                    +-----------+       +-----------+

       quorum = 2 of 3 (leader + 1 follower)  --> commit; linearization point
       read: leader lease valid --> serve 5 locally (no quorum round needed)
```

### Walkthrough
1. Client sends `write(x=5)` to the leader, which assigns log index 7 in term 3.
2. Leader fans out `AppendEntries` to both followers in parallel and waits for acks.
3. Once one follower acks, the leader has quorum (leader counts as 1 of 3) and commits.
4. The commit point is the linearization point — any future read sees x=5.
5. Client issues `read(x)`; leader's lease is still valid so it returns 5 without a quorum round.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Simplified Raft-like leader-based strong-read mock for 3 nodes.
import threading, time

class RaftNode:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
        self.log = []                 # committed entries
        self.term = 0
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

class RaftCluster:
    def __init__(self, names):
        self.nodes = [RaftNode(n) for n in names]
        self.leader_idx = 0           # node 0 wins the (mock) election
        self.lease_valid_until = 0.0

    def _quorum(self):
        return len(self.nodes) // 2 + 1   # 3 nodes -> 2

    def write(self, key, value):
        leader = self.nodes[self.leader_idx]
        new_term = leader.term + 1
        entry = (new_term, key, value)
        acks = 1                        # leader counts
        for f in self.nodes:
            if f is leader: continue
            with f.lock:                # mock RPC: AppendEntries
                f.log.append(entry)
                f.term = new_term
                acks += 1
        if acks < self._quorum():
            raise RuntimeError("no quorum -- write refused (CP)")
        with leader.lock:
            leader.log.append(entry)
            leader.term = new_term
        # refresh lease from quorum acks
        self.lease_valid_until = time.time() + 1.0
        return True

    def read_strong(self, key):
        leader = self.nodes[self.leader_idx]
        # linearizable read: must confirm leader still holds quorum
        if time.time() < self.lease_valid_until:
            # fast path: leader lease still valid, serve locally
            return self._latest(leader, key)
        # slow path: quorum read to confirm leader is current
        acks = 1
        for f in self.nodes:
            if f is leader: continue
            with f.lock:
                acks += 1              # mock heartbeat
        if acks < self._quorum():
            raise RuntimeError("no quorum -- read refused")
        self.lease_valid_until = time.time() + 1.0
        return self._latest(leader, key)

    def _latest(self, node, key):
        for term, k, v in reversed(node.log):
            if k == key:
                return v
        return None

c = RaftCluster(["A", "B", "C"])
c.write("balance", 100)
print("strong read:", c.read_strong("balance"))    # 100
c.write("balance", 75)
print("strong read:", c.read_strong("balance"))    # 75
```

quiz.explanation: Linearizability is the property that every operation appears to execute atomically at a single real-time point between invocation and response, producing a total order that respects real-time precedence — i.e., if operation A completes before B starts, then B must observe A's effect.

quiz.explanation: A leader lease is a time-bounded grant from a quorum of followers to the leader asserting that no other leader can be elected during the lease window. With an active lease, the leader knows it is still the leader and can serve linearizable reads locally without a quorum round-trip — cutting read latency from a full RPC to a local memory read.

quiz.explanation: TrueTime is Google's globally-synchronized clock API that returns an interval [earliest, latest] rather than a point, with the interval bounded to under 7ms using GPS and atomic clocks in every datacenter. Spanner needs it because pure linearizability only orders operations that overlap in real time; for non-overlapping operations (sequential writes from different clients in different DCs), linearizability is silent.

At t=0 the partition isolates the leader from the two followers.
etcd is not designed for high write throughput on a single key — its Raft log serializes all writes to the same key, so a single hot key caps throughput at the leader's…

quiz.explanation: Raft commits as soon as a quorum acks — for a three-node cluster, that is the leader plus one follower. A slow-disk follower simply falls behind; the leader commits with the healthy follower and the slow one catches up later via AppendEntries backoff. Write latency is therefore not directly affected in the steady state, but two secondary effects bite.
